source.title: Decoder-Hybrid-Decoder Architecture for Efficient Reasoning with Long Generation
source.authors: Li-Liang Ren; Congcong Chen; Hao-Ran Xu; Young Jin Kim; Adam Atkinson; Zheng Zhan; Jiankai Sun; Baolin Peng; Li-Yuan Liu; Shuo-Hang Wang; Hao Cheng; Jia-Xin Gao; Weizhu Chen; Ye-Long Shen

record.file_problem: The complete paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures validation-loss scaling with compute and training tokens and compares fitted curves across architectures and training setups. It uses power-law fitting, but evaluates new architectures and a different scaling setup rather than reproducing the original experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper fits validation loss against training FLOPs and training tokens on SlimPajama. Its compute sweep scales model size and training tokens proportionally; its data sweep holds model size at 1B parameters. It does not test a compute-optimal parameter/token allocation or verify forecasts from small runs on much larger held-out runs. Downstream benchmark scores and inference throughput are not linked to pretraining loss across scales, so they do not test V6.
record.test_reason: The paper fits held-out SlimPajama validation loss as a saturating power law of training FLOPs for five sizes (about 155M–3.4B parameters, 12.5B–342B tokens, roughly 3 orders of compute) and of tokens at fixed 1B size. It reports fit quality (R² ≥ 0.999) for new hybrid architectures and a Transformer++ baseline, in a new setting (µP++, 5× over-trained). Its Appendix E ablations show the fitted exponent and asymptote shifting with parameterization, schedule, batch rule and initialization. The scaling law is also used as a comparison tool, but these fits are reported results that bear on V1 and V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that power-law fits against FLOPs show SambaY has lower irreducible loss than baselines, including Samba+YOCO and Transformer++. All architectures share the exponent b = 0.07, and µP++ gives lower irreducible loss than SP and several ablated alternatives. They treat the extrapolated C as the main indicator of long-term scaling potential. They also note that Transformer++ reaches a similar asymptote under fixed-size data scaling, and that hyperparameters were not exhaustively tuned per architecture.
record.recipe_differences: The study fits validation loss against FLOPs and training tokens in a manner similar to scaling-law work, but uses new hybrid architectures, SlimPajama, µP++ and least-squares/LMA fitting; it does not reproduce the original model/data allocation experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported curves and outcomes vary with parameterization (µP++ versus SP or µP), batch-size scaling, initialization, learning-rate schedule, learning-rate and weight-decay scaling, embedding setup, and architecture.

fits_no_version.finding: Under µP++ compute scaling, the extrapolated irreducible loss C differs by architecture: SambaY 0.58, Transformer++ 0.64, and SambaY significantly below Samba+YOCO. The compute exponent b = 0.07 is identical across architectures. In fixed-size data scaling, Transformer++'s C (1.82) nearly matches the hybrids despite a large in-range loss gap.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architecture family (token mixer) shifts the fitted loss asymptote but not the compute exponent under a shared hyperparameter-transfer scheme.

fits_no_version.finding: Original µP with tied embeddings diverged (NaN) after 204K steps at 600B tokens, while µP++ trained stably.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Hyperparameter-transfer scheme determines whether long over-trained runs remain stable enough to follow a scaling curve.

record.problems: The scaling evidence is limited to the stated datasets and training setups. The compute sweep changes model size and token count proportionally, so their independent effects are not isolated there. The text provides only some exact fitted values; many comparisons are described qualitatively or shown in figures. No confidence intervals for fitted exponents or asymptotes are stated, and the authors acknowledge that architecture-specific hyperparameter searches were not exhaustive.
record.rows_left_out: No result bearing on the listed versions was left out. Downstream benchmark scores and throughput results were omitted because they do not test scaling-law prediction or a relation between pretraining loss and downstream performance.

untested.parts: No pure parameter-count sweep with data non-bottlenecked. The token sweep spans under one order of magnitude. Params and tokens are scaled together in the compute sweep.
No forecast from small runs is checked against held-out larger runs. Extrapolated asymptotes C are not validated.
There is no compute-optimal search; the token count is fixed at 5× the Chinchilla ratio by design.
Depth and width are not varied independently at a fixed parameter count; the aspect ratio is fixed by rule.
Downstream scores are reported only at single scales and are not related to scale or loss.
Fitting method, parameter-counting convention, and bending away from a single power law are not tested.

missing.what: Numeric C and b values for the SP curves and for the Samba+YOCO, SWA+YOCO and other architectures in Figure 2; only figures show them.
Numeric fit parameters for the µP++ ablations (batch scaling, normal init, WSD, LR scaling + independent WD, untied embeddings).
Model sizes and token counts defining the compute sweep range (155M–3.4B params, 12.5B–342B tokens).

record.verdict_notes: This is primarily an architecture paper that uses scaling fits as a comparison tool. Its architecture rankings rest on extrapolated asymptotes C from at most ~3 orders of compute, which the paper does not validate on larger runs. The two sweeps give very different C (0.58–0.64 vs 1.82), which shows how sensitive C is to the sweep design. V4 links were removed because the comparison is across token-mixer families, not depth/width shape. The study is not an original source for any version.

versions.untested_parts: The study measures loss against compute and tokens, but does not independently sweep parameter count while holding tokens and compute non-bottlenecked.
No held-out prediction of much larger runs from fits on smaller runs is evaluated.
No loss-minimizing parameter/token split is searched or fitted as a function of compute.
Architecture comparisons use parameter-matched designs and scaling curves, but do not systematically vary depth and width independently over a wide range.
The scaling experiments concern text language-model pretraining; other modalities, repeated-data regimes, fine-tuning, and transfer are not tested.
Downstream benchmarks are reported for selected models, but the study does not test whether their performance is predictably related to scale or pretraining loss.

The study varies parameterization, batch scaling, initialization, learning-rate scaling, embedding setup, and learning-rate schedule; it does not compare power-law fitting algorithms or parameter-count conventions.

rows.check: NaN divergence after 204K steps is a training-stability outcome, not a change in fitted exponent or allocation. It does not measure V7's fit-dependence.

rows.subject: Transformer++ with µP++ and untied embeddings
rows.operation_detail: Compare tied and untied embedding setups.
rows.measure: Validation loss at 100B tokens and fitted irreducible loss
rows.value: Untied embeddings have significantly lower validation loss at 100B tokens, while irreducible loss remains comparable.
rows.note: The paper attributes the early improvement to faster convergence rather than a better fitted asymptote.
rows.check: Untied embeddings lower loss at 100B tokens but leave the asymptote C comparable. The fit shifts in convergence rate only, not in asymptote.
